title: Before we begin
hookLine: the next sessions tell of the Holocaust, the Shoah; go slowly and stop whenever you need

cards: Before a hard conversation, people often pause at the door. They take a breath. They put down whatever they were carrying.

That's what today is. The next sessions on this path tell of the Holocaust, the murder of Europe's Jews by Nazi Germany and those who helped it. Some listeners carry this history in their own families.
Some are meeting it closely for the first time. Either way, it is heavy. So today there is no history lesson.
Just a word, a way of walking, and permission to stop.

teach.h: SHOAH: A BIBLICAL WORD FOR RUIN.
teach.b: Shoah is a Hebrew word. It is the name Jews in Israel, and Jews elsewhere too, use for the Holocaust. It is not a new word.
It appears in the Bible, where the prophet Zephaniah describes a day of ruin and desolation, a day of darkness: a biblical word for devastation, carried forward to name what happened.
Some people use the English word Holocaust. Some prefer Shoah, a word from their own language and their own Scripture. Both are used, with respect.
Now, the way of walking. The Bible has a picture of how to come near great suffering.
When Job has lost almost everything, three friends come to comfort him. And the first thing they do is not speak.
The text says they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and no one said a word, because they saw how great his pain was. Silence first. Words later.
That is how these sessions will try to go. They will tell real history, honestly and with care. They will begin with how people lived, not only how they died.
They will say names when names are known. They will not use horror to hold your attention.

teach.h: YOU MAY STOP WHENEVER YOU NEED.
teach.b: And the most important part: you may stop whenever you need. You may skip a day and come back. You may listen with someone beside you.
Going slowly is not failing. In this history, going gently is a way of honoring the people in it.

how: Jewish communities remember the Shoah on Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day, with candles, the reading of names, survivors' testimony and memorial prayers; in Israel a siren sounds and people stand in silence.

o: tell him it will get better.

practice: Ask yourself a few plain questions, and let the answers come slowly: what time of day is best for listening to something heavy, and who could you talk to if a session stays with you?
What helps you come back to yourself: a walk, a cup of tea, a call, a prayer, if you pray? Choose one thing to do after each of the next sessions.
